Chapter 6: The Art of Selective Execution—Making Essentialism Happen.
Now that you’ve got your priorities straight and your boundaries set, it’s time to turn your intentions into real action. This is where selective execution comes in. Think of it as focusing your energy on just the handful of things that truly matter—and making sure they actually get done.
It’s not enough to simply know what’s essential. The real difference comes from following through, day after day.
So, how do you make this work in your everyday life? It starts with making the path to action as simple as possible. That means clearing away anything that gets in your way or adds friction. Let’s say deep work is at the top of your list—just imagine how much easier it’ll be if you take a few minutes to tidy up your workspace, silence your phone, and gather what you need before you even begin. The idea is simple: make the right action the easiest one to take.
Here are a few ways you can streamline execution:
First, break big projects into small, clear next steps. That way, you always know exactly what to do next.
Second, schedule your most essential tasks for those times when your energy is at its peak—maybe that’s first thing in the morning, or right after a coffee break.
And third, use checklists or visual cues to keep yourself on track. Sometimes, just seeing a reminder can nudge you to take the next step.
Another important piece is building in buffers—giving yourself some extra time and space around the activities that matter most. Life is full of surprises, and you never know when something urgent will pop up. By adding a little slack to your schedule, you protect your top priorities from being pushed aside. Picture a manager who sets aside extra time before and after key meetings—not just to prepare, but to reflect afterward, instead of rushing from one thing to the next.
Selective execution also means getting comfortable with saying no—even to good opportunities that just aren’t the best fit. It can be tough, especially when you’re tempted by interesting projects or requests from people you admire. But holding firm to what’s essential means your time and energy are always spent where they’ll make the biggest difference.
I love the image of a gardener tending a small, carefully chosen plot. Instead of trying to grow everything, the gardener picks just a few plants, giving them all the care and attention they need to flourish. And the harvest? It’s richer and far more rewarding.
When you put selective execution into practice, you’re making the essential visible and actionable every single day. It’s all about asking yourself, over and over: “What’s the most important thing I can do right now?”
Stick with this habit, and you’ll see real progress, feel less weighed down by stress, and enjoy a deeper sense of accomplishment in everything you do.
